events.label: Alexandre Pétion bankrolls the liberation
events.description: Alexandre Pétion — the free-born, French-educated man of color who governed southern Haiti after Dessalines's assassination — received the broken exile Bolívar in 1816 and gave him everything: ships, weapons, ammunition, a printing press, and men. He asked, almost, for nothing.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Pétion was a different kind of Haitian leader from the warrior Dessalines — a politician who divided the land among the peasantry and ran his republic as the 'good father' (le bon Papa), and who understood that Haiti's safety depended on abolition spreading across the hemisphere so it would no longer be a lone target. His one condition on the aid was that Bolívar free the slaves wherever he won; his one request was that his own role stay quiet, lest the European powers find a pretext to crush the isolated black republic. He largely got his wish — for over a century the official statues of the Liberator left out the Haitian who armed him. The generosity is the more striking because Haiti was poor and surrounded by enemies, yet it bankrolled the freedom of the very mainland that would mostly repay it with silence and ostracism.

events.label: The Tumult of Aranjuez topples Charles IV
events.description: A revolt of courtiers, soldiers, and townspeople against the king's hated favorite, the minister Manuel Godoy, spilled over into toppling Charles IV himself, forcing him to abdicate in favor of his son Ferdinand VII — just weeks before Napoleon lured both to Bayonne.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Godoy was the lightning rod. A handsome former royal guardsman who had risen through the queen's favor to run the country with the grandiose title 'Prince of the Peace,' he was blamed for Spain's humiliations and for letting French armies into the country — and the mob that ransacked his palace at Aranjuez was after his head. Ferdinand, the heir, had been intriguing against his own father for years and rode the riot to the throne. The whole sordid family melodrama is what handed Napoleon his opening: a king pushed out by a palace mob, a son who'd plotted to replace him, the two of them feuding in public. Napoleon simply offered to referee the quarrel at Bayonne — and pocketed the crown. The revolt meant to save Spain from a bad minister instead delivered it to a French emperor.

events.label: Joseph Bonaparte is installed on the Spanish throne
events.description: Napoleon handed the crown of Spain to his own brother Joseph Bonaparte, who reigned as José I over a country that overwhelmingly refused to accept him. The rejection of the French usurper — in favor of the captive Ferdinand — is what launched the juntas, in Spain and across the Americas alike.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Joseph was not the cartoon tyrant the propaganda made him. He had already been a competent king of Naples, he tried to govern Spain as a genuine reformer — abolishing the Inquisition, curbing feudal dues, pushing a constitution — and modern historians treat him far more kindly than his subjects did. But none of it mattered, because to Spaniards he was simply the brother of the man who'd stolen their king. They nicknamed him 'Pepe Botella' ('Joe Bottle'), smearing him as a drunk though he barely drank, and his real authority never reached much beyond wherever French bayonets happened to stand. His reign is the clearest proof that the empire ran on legitimacy, not administration: a more capable government than Ferdinand's ever provided could not buy a day of loyalty, because it sat on a stolen throne.

events.label: The Caribbean sugar economy consumes lives
events.description: Caribbean sugar was a death machine. It was cheaper to work an enslaved person to death within a few years and buy a replacement off a slave ship than to keep one alive — so the plantations devoured people, importing tens of thousands of fresh captives a year to replace the ones they killed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: This is the single fact that separates Caribbean slavery from the slavery of the North American mainland, where the enslaved population grew on its own across generations. In the sugar islands it did the opposite: the work — cutting cane in tropical heat, then feeding it into crushing mills and boiling houses where exhaustion and accidents maimed and killed — was so lethal that the enslaved population could not reproduce itself and had to be constantly topped up from Africa. The casual modern word 'slavery' barely conveys it. Sugar was the oil of the eighteenth century, and Europe's sweet tooth was paid for in lives consumed at industrial speed. The enslaved majority of Saint-Domingue knew exactly what the system was, which is why, when they rose, they did not negotiate — they burned the cane fields that were burning them.
